FIRST WARN FORECAST
Wednesday, August 19, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

HEAVY RAIN AND STORMS THIS MORNING

It is a wet and stormy start to Wednesday across portions of Missouri and Illinois, and showers and thunderstorms will continue through at least the morning hours. The greatest coverage will generally be along and south of I-70 in Missouri and I-64 in Illinois.

The primary concern this morning is locally heavy rainfall. Some locations across central and southeast Missouri could receive 2 to 3 inches or more in a relatively narrow corridor. Because thunderstorms may repeatedly move across some of the same areas, localized flash flooding is possible through the morning.

This will not be a widespread flooding event for everyone, but where the heavier thunderstorms repeatedly track, rainfall can add up quickly. Watch low-lying areas, creeks, poor drainage locations, and roads that are prone to flooding.

Some storms may also produce gusty winds this morning. However, the current storm structure has been largely outflow-dominant, which should make it somewhat more difficult for the strongest winds aloft to reach the surface.

The widespread rain should gradually become less organized later this morning, although scattered showers may linger around the I-70 corridor through midday.

ANOTHER ROUND POSSIBLE THIS AFTERNOON

Unfortunately, we may not be completely finished once the morning storms move away.

Additional scattered showers and thunderstorms are possible this afternoon and evening, with two areas getting most of our attention.

The first is northeast Missouri into west-central Illinois. Some of our short-range guidance suggests thunderstorms could move southeast into this area during the afternoon. If we can get some breaks in the clouds and enough instability develops, a few of these storms could become strong to severe.

Large hail and damaging winds would be the primary concerns across northeast Missouri and west-central Illinois. There is considerable uncertainty regarding exactly how these storms evolve, so this is an area we will need to monitor throughout the day.

The second area is southeast Missouri into southwest Illinois.

The position of the effective frontal boundary will be critical. Right now, I think the boundary will probably settle somewhere near the Missouri-Arkansas border. If it stays that far south, the greater severe weather threat would remain south of our coverage area.

However, it is going to be close.

Additional thunderstorms could develop near the boundary late this afternoon into the early evening and potentially affect portions of southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. If storms develop in a favorable environment, damaging winds would be the primary threat.

A few storms could also take on supercell characteristics. If that happens, marginally severe hail and even a brief tornado cannot be completely ruled out near the boundary. The tornado threat is low, but it is not zero.

A COMPLICATED SEVERE WEATHER FORECAST

I want to emphasize that confidence in exactly how this afternoon and evening evolves is fairly low.

What happens this morning will have a significant influence on what happens later today. How quickly the morning rain moves out, where clouds clear, where instability can rebuild, and exactly where the frontal boundary settles will determine where stronger thunderstorms can develop.

There may also be a small-scale disturbance moving across northeast Missouri and west-central Illinois this afternoon that could help spark additional thunderstorms.

In other words, there are several moving pieces on the weather board today.

The overall chance for additional thunderstorms this afternoon and evening is around 40 to 60 percent in our two main areas of concern: northeast Missouri into west-central Illinois and southeast Missouri into southwest Illinois.

Not everyone will see another thunderstorm this afternoon. But where storms develop, a few could become strong to severe.

QUIETER WEATHER RETURNS THURSDAY

The good news is that once we get through Wednesday, our weather becomes considerably quieter.

High pressure will move into the Mid-Mississippi Valley Thursday and Friday, bringing dry conditions to central Missouri, the St. Louis metro, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois.

Temperatures will remain near to slightly below normal, with highs generally in the 80s. Humidity should also remain much more tolerable than the oppressive conditions we experienced earlier this month.

There are no signs of a major heat wave returning through the end of the work week.

WEEKEND STILL LOOKING COMFORTABLE

The weekend forecast remains somewhat dependent on how a larger upper-level system develops across the Great Lakes.

One group of our ensemble guidance brings a stronger trough farther west, which would send another push of cooler air into Missouri and Illinois while keeping us mostly dry.

Another solution keeps that trough weaker and farther east. That scenario would leave us closer to the edge of the cooler air and could eventually open the door for a complex of thunderstorms sometime Sunday night into Monday morning.

At this point, I favor temperatures remaining near or slightly below normal through the weekend. Saturday currently looks like the better bet for widespread dry weather, while we will continue watching Sunday night into Monday for the possibility of our next round of thunderstorms.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Wednesday is another day to remain weather aware.

Widespread showers and thunderstorms will continue through the morning, particularly along and south of I-70 in Missouri and I-64 in Illinois. Locally heavy rainfall could produce 2 to 3 inches or more in a few locations, creating an isolated flash flooding threat across portions of central and southeast Missouri.

Additional thunderstorms are possible this afternoon and evening. The two areas we are watching most closely are northeast Missouri into west-central Illinois and southeast Missouri into southwest Illinois.

A few storms could become strong to severe. Damaging winds are the primary overall concern, although large hail is possible with stronger storms across northeast Missouri and west-central Illinois. A brief tornado cannot be completely ruled out near the frontal boundary across the far southeastern portion of the region.

There is quite a bit of uncertainty with the afternoon forecast, so we will be watching radar and trends closely as the morning storms move through.

Then we finally settle things down.

Thursday and Friday look dry and comfortable, and temperatures should remain near to slightly below normal into the weekend.

severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

Central Illinois
Areas northeast of Springfield, Illinois
Greatest potential for strong tornadoes and destructive winds

St. Louis Metro
West-central Illinois
Southwest Illinois

Southern Missouri
South-central Missouri
Southeast Missouri
Southern Illinois
Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.
